tldr: NestDex dramatically streamlines data collection for dexterous multi-fingered hands by using learned hand skills (a copilot) and a 1-DoF clutch, then trains an autonomous policy directly controlling both the arm and hand from the collected high-quality demonstrations.
hero_caption: System architecture and demonstration collection pipeline of NestDex. Camera-based finger retargeting trains single-skill inner policies, which act as a copilot during teleoperation guided by a clutch and a VLM selector. The collected full-task demonstrations train an end-to-end outer visuomotor policy that does not require inner policies at deployment.
overview:
Dexterous manipulation using multi-fingered hands holds great promise for substantially expanding what robots can do. However, when using imitation learning to achieve this, the biggest bottleneck is collecting high-quality demonstration data. While parallel-jaw grippers require only a single degree of freedom for opening and closing, multi-fingered hands possess a dozen to over 20 joints in the hand alone. It is extremely difficult for a human operator to teleoperate delicate fingertip contacts while simultaneously moving the arm.

To address this challenge, the authors divided the labor: the human guides overall task-level arm movement, while complex fingertip contact behaviors are delegated to pre-learned hand skills. This is the core idea of NestDex. During teleoperation, the operator simply squeezes or releases a 1-DoF clutch to advance or rewind the progress of the active inner policy (hand skill). In addition, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) automatically switches to the appropriate skill for each task stage based on wrist camera images.

From these full-task demonstrations, an autonomous outer policy is trained to control both the arm and hand together. At deployment time, the inner policies are no longer needed. The authors also introduce a hand-action variational autoencoder (H-VAE) that compresses the 20-DoF hand commands into a 10-dimensional latent space to make policy learning much easier.

Across real-world experiments evaluated on six tasks—including complex tasks that were impossible to collect with conventional retargeting teleoperation (AnyTeleop)—NestDex dramatically improved demonstration success rates and time efficiency. Furthermore, the autonomous policies trained on the collected data achieved high success rates.
contributions: Proposed a copilot-assisted teleoperation system that uses a 1-DoF reversible clutch to advance and rewind state-adaptive hand skills, combined with a VLM for automatic skill switching.

Constructed a nested learning framework that uses inner hand policies (copilot) only during demonstration collection, removing them at deployment to control the arm and hand directly with a single autonomous outer visuomotor policy.
Introduced H-VAE to compress high-dimensional hand joint commands into a low-dimensional latent space, providing compact targets for imitation learning.

Quantitatively demonstrated significant improvements in data collection efficiency and reliability across six real-world dexterous tasks, highlighting the importance of temporal ensembling in closed-loop execution.

sections.heading: Why is teleoperating multi-fingered hands so difficult?
sections.summary: Imitation learning depends heavily on consistent demonstration data, but it is extremely difficult for a human to simultaneously coordinate arm trajectories and multi-joint contact behaviors. NestDex proposes a new framework where the human guides arm progress while learned inner policies handle fingertip contact motions.
sections.details:
Imitation learning has achieved remarkable results in robot manipulation, but its success relies heavily on the consistency and completeness of demonstration data collected by human operators.

For a standard parallel-jaw gripper, hand control is as simple as deciding a single coordinate for opening or closing. With a multi-fingered hand, however, an operator must coordinate a massive number of joints simultaneously to establish contact, maintain it, and prevent slipping. The operator has to advance the overall task with the arm while continuously regulating delicate contact states with the fingers. As the task becomes more dexterous, the difficulty of data collection skyrockets.

Existing teleoperation systems, such as retargeting human hands from cameras or motion-capture gloves, tend to prioritize hand expressiveness at the expense of operator cognitive load. This work proposes a fundamentally different division of labor: the operator focuses on macro-level arm guidance and overall task progress, delegating delicate fingertip contact motions to reusable inner hand policies (hand skills).

The operator simply regulates a 1-DoF clutch to advance the inner policy's behavior or rewind it if something goes wrong. When the task phase transitions, a vision-language model (VLM) selector automatically switches to the appropriate skill. The resulting full-task demonstrations are then used to train a single outer visuomotor policy that operates autonomously without relying on the inner policies.

Top left shows tongs transfer and simultaneous dual-object grasping with the learned autonomous policy; top right shows a single grasp skill adapting to diverse object geometries; bottom shows demonstration collection for bimanual tasks (binder binding and toaster cooking).

sections.heading: At the intersection of dexterous teleoperation, hierarchical learning, and latent action representations
sections.summary: This section examines three key research areas: dexterous teleoperation, hierarchical policy learning and skill selection, and latent representations of high-dimensional actions. NestDex combines these concepts while standing out by using skills solely during data collection and collapsing into a single flat policy at deployment.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main technological foundations:

- Dexterous teleoperation and demonstration collection:
Retargeting human hand motions onto robot hands has been widely studied. Methods include motion capture gloves and vision-based hand pose estimation (such as AnyTeleop), but both require the operator to continuously specify all arm and finger joints simultaneously. While shared autonomy approaches that delegate hand control to policies have been explored, NestDex fully integrates this division of labor into complete-task demonstration collection.

- Hierarchical and skill-based policy learning:
To tackle long-horizon, complex tasks, numerous studies combine reusable low-level skills with high-level policies or Large Language Model (LLM) agents that switch between them. However, most existing approaches keep this hierarchical structure (the selector and individual skills) active even after deployment in the real world. In contrast, NestDex treats the skill selector and inner policies purely as copilot scaffolding to aid demonstration collection, deploying a flat, single visuomotor policy at test time.

- Latent action representations for dexterous policy learning:
Because the joint space of multi-fingered hands is high-dimensional, exploration in reinforcement learning and supervised action prediction in imitation learning become challenging. While prior work compresses or discretizes action spaces, NestDex applies a variational autoencoder (H-VAE) exclusively to hand joint commands while retaining arm commands in joint space, balancing precise arm positioning with coordinated finger patterns.

sections.heading: Basics of action chunking and temporal ensembling
sections.summary: The policies in this work use action chunking to predict multiple future action steps from current observations. By querying the policy at every step and computing an exponentially weighted average over overlapping trajectories (temporal ensembling), the robot achieves smooth motion.
sections.details:
Both the visuomotor policy and proprioceptive policy used in this study output predictions in the form of action chunks.

At time $t$, given observations, policy $\pi_\theta$ does not predict a single action; instead, it outputs an action sequence over a horizon of $H$ steps: $\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_t = [\widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{t\mid t}, \dots, \widehat{\mathbf{a}}_{t+H-1\mid t}]$. Predicting actions in blocks makes it easier to capture short-term temporal coordination across fingers and effectively shortens the decision-making horizon.

However, if the system executes a chunk to completion before fetching the next observation, it reacts slowly to environmental changes or contact events, resulting in jerky motions at chunk boundaries. To avoid this, NestDex queries the policy at every control step so that past and newly predicted chunks overlap.

When multiple predictions exist for time step $t$, temporal ensembling averages them with exponential weighting from older to newer predictions. The executed action $\mathbf{a}_t^{\mathrm{exec}}$ is computed as:
$$\mathbf{a}_t^{\mathrm{exec}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \mathcal{P}_t[i]}{\sum_i w_i}, \quad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$$
where $i$ is the age index of the prediction (0 being the oldest) and $m > 0$ is the decay parameter. Selecting a smaller $m$ gives higher weight to predictions informed by the latest observations. This mechanism incorporates fresh contact feedback while preventing discontinuous command jumps, producing smooth fingertip motions.

sections.heading: How NestDex works: from inner skill learning to the outer autonomous policy
sections.summary: Inner hand policies are trained on retargeted multi-view camera data, then assist teleoperation via a reversible clutch and a VLM selector. The collected full-task data is used with H-VAE to compress hand actions, training an outer policy that jointly controls the arm and hand.
sections.details:
NestDex features a nested structure that strictly separates demonstration assistance from autonomous deployment. The setup consists of a leader side (operator) and follower side (robot), using a 7-DoF arm and 1-DoF clutch on the leader to control a 7-DoF arm and 20-DoF multi-fingered hand on the follower.

### IV-A Inner Policy Learning
First, basic hand skills needed for tasks (such as grasp, pinch, and press) are trained individually.
- Collecting hand skill demonstrations: Multiple calibrated cameras reconstruct 3D human hand landmarks, which are retargeted to the follower hand. Building on AnyTeleop, an optimization problem with a robust Huber loss, hand scale ratio $\alpha$, and temporal smoothness penalty $\beta$ is solved to produce target joint angles $\mathbf{q}_t^*$. During these motions, joint positions $\mathbf{q}$ and joint efforts $\mathbf{e}$ are recorded.
- Training the inner policy: A Transformer model takes the recent $h$ steps of proprioceptive history $\mathbf{x}_t = [\mathbf{q}_t, \mathbf{e}_t]$ and outputs an action chunk of joint positions for the next $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ steps. It relies entirely on joint position and effort histories without images, adapting to contact based on proprioception alone. For example, a single "grasp skill" is trained on just 10 trajectories collected while touching four objects (a toy leek, plastic bottle, radish, and paper cup).

### IV-B Copilot Assisted Teleoperation
During complete-task demonstration collection, the operator steers the arm while guiding the active inner policy using the clutch.
- Clutch-regulated progress: The clutch squeeze $c_t$ is mapped to a normalized skill progress $p_t \in [0, 1]$, defining a target execution index $s_t^{\mathrm{in}} = \lfloor p_t (T_{\max}-1) \rfloor$. The current execution index $r_t^{\mathrm{in}}$ tracks this target by one step at a time. Squeezing the clutch steps the policy forward and recomputes chunks from the latest contact history, while releasing it plays the buffer backward to rewind motion. This allows the operator to instantly retry failed contact attempts.
- Automatic skill selection via VLM: Images from the wrist camera and skill descriptions are passed to a pre-trained VLM agent, which automatically selects the appropriate hand skill for the current phase. Skill transitions are only triggered when the clutch is fully released ($r_t^{\mathrm{in}} = 0$), preventing unintended switching during skill execution.

### IV-C Outer Policy Learning
Using the collected full-task demonstrations, an autonomous policy is trained for deployment.
- Hand-VAE (H-VAE): Directly imitating 20-DoF hand joint commands $\mathbf{a}_k^{\mathrm{hand}}$ leads to overfitting and instability due to high dimensionality. NestDex uses a VAE to compress only the hand commands into a 10-dimensional latent representation $\mathbf{z}_k$, while keeping the arm's 7-DoF joint commands intact.
- Outer policy training and deployment: A visuomotor Transformer is trained to predict future $H$-step chunks of arm commands and latent hand actions from camera images $\mathbf{v}_t$ and robot states $\mathbf{s}_t$. At deployment, the predicted latent actions are decoded back into 20-DoF hand joint targets by the H-VAE decoder. The inner policies and VLM selector are completely bypassed.

captions.F5: Hand action compression (H-VAE) and outer policy training/deployment architecture. (a) An offline VAE compresses 20-DoF hand targets into a 10-DoF latent space and reconstructs them. (b) The outer policy predicts arm targets and latent hand actions from camera images and states, which the decoder reconstructs into full hand targets at deployment.

sections.heading: Real-robot experiments: thorough evaluation of efficiency, autonomy, and contact adaptation
sections.summary: Experiments across six dexterous manipulation tasks demonstrated that NestDex significantly improves demonstration time and success rates over baselines, yielding autonomous policies with high success rates. Ablations validated the necessity of H-VAE dimensionality reduction and temporal ensembling.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a real-robot setup featuring a 7-DoF Piper Nero arm and 1-DoF clutch on the leader side, and a matching arm, 20-DoF WujiHand I (five-fingered hand), and wrist camera on the follower side.

### V-A Demonstration Collection Reliability and Efficiency (Q1)
NestDex was compared against AnyTeleop, a strong real-time hand-tracking baseline, across six tasks (20 trials each).
In AnyTeleop, complex tasks such as "Tongs Transfer" (withdrawing tongs from a stand and picking up a carrot) and bimanual tasks suffered a 0% success rate, making demonstration collection impossible. In contrast, NestDex achieved dramatically higher success rates and significantly reduced collection time per successful demonstration across all comparable tasks, even when factoring in the preparation time for inner policies. Separating arm guidance from finger coordination proved highly effective.

### V-B From Copilot to Autonomy & Effect of H-VAE (Q2, Q3)
Outer visuomotor policies were trained on 20 successful demonstrations per task and evaluated over 20 autonomous rollouts each.
Policies trained on NestDex demonstrations outperformed those trained on AnyTeleop data across all tasks. For Tongs Transfer, which could not even be demonstrated under AnyTeleop, NestDex successfully achieved autonomous execution.
Evaluating the role of H-VAE action compression (Q3), predicting 10-DoF latent variables consistently outperformed directly predicting 20-DoF joint angles across all tasks. Bundling high-dimensional finger coordination patterns into a compact latent space substantially stabilizes imitation learning from limited demonstrations.

### V-C Analysis of Online Execution and Contact Behavior (Q4, Q5)
Control loop dynamics were analyzed in depth during bottle grasping.
- Importance of closed-loop adaptation: A "Fixed replay" baseline that simply replayed a successful joint trajectory succeeded in only 3/10 trials, whereas closed-loop control that re-predicted actions from the latest proprioceptive history achieved 9/10 successes ($p = 0.0198$). While fixed replays fail under slight positional misalignments, closed-loop execution senses contact forces and adapts finger closure accordingly.
- Smoothing with temporal ensembling: Without temporal ensembling in closed-loop execution, the 95th-percentile jerk was 2.30 times higher than with ensembling ($p = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$), causing sustained excessive effort after contact. Temporal ensembling plays a decisive role in producing smooth contacts.
- Shape adaptation: Although the inner grasp policy receives only proprioceptive state (position and effort) without images, it naturally adapted its final finger configuration to contact reaction forces across hard bottles and soft paper cups.

### V-D Skill Reuse across Task Stages (Q6)
In long-horizon tasks such as toaster cooking and binder binding, the VLM reliably switched between appropriate inner skills (tongs grasp, button press, plate hold) based on the task stage, reusing the same skill when required.

(b) Grouping fingers to grasp two blocks simultaneously and deposit them into a trash bin. Both execute autonomously at test time without inner policies.
captions.F7: Ablation study of temporal ensembling during bottle grasping. (a)(b) show 95th-percentile jerk of executed commands and pre-limit commands, where temporal ensembling (green) achieves the smoothest execution. (c) shows the ratio indicating that omitting ensembling produces 2 to 3 times higher jerk across various filter window lengths.

sections.heading: Conclusion: a path to teaching dexterous manipulation without operator burden
sections.summary: NestDex overcomes the fundamental bottleneck of multi-fingered teleoperation by incorporating reusable, contact-adaptive hand skills as a data-collection copilot. Compressing high-dimensional hand actions enables effective imitation learning from high-quality demonstrations, unlocking fully autonomous dexterous manipulation.
sections.details:
In dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands, the bottleneck has not been the expressiveness of policy networks, but the sheer difficulty of collecting consistent demonstrations that coordinate the arm with complex finger motions.

NestDex elegantly solves this problem by placing contact-adaptive inner hand skills inside the demonstration collection loop, narrowing the operator's role to task-level arm movement and clutch-regulated progress. Real-world experiments proved that this approach dramatically improves demonstration reliability and time efficiency, and the resulting outer policies achieve advanced autonomous behaviors such as tool use and simultaneous multi-object grasping.

Furthermore, the findings show that compressing hand action spaces with H-VAE strongly facilitates imitation learning, while closed-loop proprioceptive feedback paired with temporal ensembling is indispensable for smooth contact adaptation. NestDex provides a practical and powerful end-to-end pipeline from teleoperation to full autonomy for dexterous hands.

takeaways: In multi-fingered teleoperation, separating global arm movement (guided by a human) from finger contact behaviors (managed by pre-trained skills) via a 1-DoF clutch is exceptionally effective.

The inner skills and VLM used during teleoperation do not need to remain at deployment; the robot can be fully automated by training a single end-to-end visuomotor policy from the collected demonstrations.

Rather than imitating raw joint commands for hands with over 20 DoFs, compressing them into a ~10-dimensional latent space using a VAE dramatically stabilizes learning with small demonstration datasets.

For hand skills involving contact, combining closed-loop proprioceptive prediction (position and effort) with temporal ensembling (exponentially weighted chunk averaging) is essential to achieve smooth, robust contact adaptation.
limitations: The contact adaptability of the inner policies depends on the contact conditions present in their training data, meaning they do not zero-shot generalize to completely unseen shapes or extreme physical property shifts.
There is an upfront cost of collecting roughly 10 demonstrations and pre-training an inner policy for each required primitive skill (e.g., grasping, pressing) before starting full-task teleoperation.
VLM skill switching is restricted to moments when the clutch is fully released (zero progress), precluding seamless, dynamic skill transitions in the middle of ongoing motions.
